Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Redi.
I'm your host, Eddie Palmgen, and with me in the studio is my friend and colleague, Nicholas Savos.
In today's episode, we are joined by Tobias Carlisle.
Tobias is an investor and fellow podcast host with his value after hours, that he runs with a former guest of ours, Jake Taylor.
Tobias is also an author of multiple books. So, Nicholas, which one will we speak about today?
So today we will speak about the acquires multiple. This is a book that is a condensed version of
of the earlier books that Tobias has written. And in the book, he described the philosophy of
deep value investing and the factors he use in his quantitative approach to investing, called the
Acquires Multiple. I think it's an eye-opener, as it discusses how most investors actually perform
worse by adding an analysis of the business in addition to what the Acquires Multiple tells
you. The Acquires Multiple was published in 2017 by Ballimore Publishing, and we are honored
to have its author on the show today. Here comes our conversation with Tobias, Carlis.
Hello, and welcome to Investing Buy the Books podcast. Thank you for having me. It's great to have you on
and thank you for taking the time. Where are you located this time? I'm in Los Angeles,
in California, in the US. In your home office or another place? Yeah, this is my, this is my
home office. I had an office, but I let it go during the pandemic and I just prefer
working from home, so I'm going to continue doing that.
And for those not familiar with you, maybe you can share a few words about your background and what led
you into the world of investing?
Sure. I'm Australian. I was a lawyer. I started practicing law in 2000, April 2000, which was right
at the very peak of the dot com 1.0 boom. And I thought that I was going in to work on venture
capital type investments. I really liked venture capital. It was very fadish, very fashionable
at the time. I like startups and venture capital and that kind of stuff. And the first day in the office
was sort of the peak and then it all sort of fell away and pretty quickly, none of the venture capital deals
were getting done. And the market was, um, got crushed. And so a lot of the work that I did was,
was working on sort of, there, a lot of these businesses failed. And so I worked
on, you know, you know, cleaning up that mess. But as that sort of happened, some of these companies had gone
public with, and they had raised a lot of money, but they were burning cash, which is very common
for early stage businesses in, in booms like that. And there were these investors
who would come along and get control of these companies and use the cash to either buy out
all the other shareholders or they'd then use the company as a platform to acquire other similar companies.
And I watched a few people do that.
And I had a little bit of trouble understanding what they were doing because I had read all of Buffett's
letters and security analysis and the intelligent investor.
And I was very much a wonderful company at a fair price kind of investor.
Or that was my.
I wasn't really investing at that point. That was my sort of mindset. And I realized that, of course, what they were trying to do is get control of the cash. Eventually, it wasn't initially kind of obvious to me that that was the case. And so I went back to security analysis because I had remembered that there were these very obscure chapters. I think it's like Chapter 28, 29, where they talk about the liquidation value of the company. And then immediately after that is sort of the relationship of the relationship of shareholders and directors.
in these sort of instances when the company is undervalued, and I realized that that was what they were doing.
And I thought it was very interesting and it sort of quickly, it was only a very short period of time.
It was only about a year or 18 months that that that happened.
And I thought next time that happens, I will, I'll try and participate in it because I realize that it only happens very
occasionally.
Most of the time, the market is too expensive and those opportunities just don't exist.
And so I continue.
I got transferred to the U.S. to San Francisco because I had a sort of technology telecommunications
background. And I worked in San Francisco on acquisitions of acquisitions of technologies. And I worked in San Francisco on acquisitions of technology. And then I had listed a company in Australia, which was a telecommunications company that did dark fiber and peering networks and those sort of infrastructure for telecommunications and internet backbone
stuff. And eventually that business was sold in 2008 and the founders made a lot of money. And I, at that time, at that time, the market, was getting close to a bottom, which happened in 2009. And so I resigned, well, the
business was sold. I was working in a little fund that was doing sort of activist-activist-type investment
and I worked there for a few years and then started my own little fund in Australia, trying to find net-nets.
In 2010, they weren't a lot around, so I had to sort of evolve my investment strategy a little
little bit, and so I went from net-n-nets to more of a sort of private equity approach, which I
had read this document written by this investment bank called Piper Jaffrey and it
was called The Endangered Species Report or Hunting Endangered Species Report and the idea was that there
were these companies that were too small to fit into the Russell 2000. They had fallen below the Russell 2000.
But by any other sort of metric, they were very, very good businesses that were growing very
fast, they were controlled by a family, they were making lots of money, but they were
just ignored by these indexes and they couldn't get any attention from institutional
shareholders and as a result, they were all undervalued. And that was probably what created the activist boom.
And so I became very interested in that and did some research and started writing about it on a
blog called Greenbacked. And through Greenbacked, I met my co-author Wes Gray,
and we wrote a book called Quantitative Value that came out in 2012.
Quantitative Value, we went in fact, under every little bit of industry and academic research that we could find.
And we tested it in a system.
So he was at Booth, which was the Chicago School of Business, a very good quantitative school in the States.
We went and tested all of these old ideas, and we were looking at things that were from the 1930s, you know, these metrics for manufacturing businesses.
from the 1930s where they had these, someone had just done a, like, a linear
regression of the various things that indicate when a company might be getting into trouble.
And they had all these funny little coefficients besides, you know, days inventory outstanding
or days' payables or any of those sort of things. And we tested them and found the things
that worked and the things that didn't work and altered them a little bit to sort of
make them, bring them up to date and publish that book.
and I've been sort of writing books and running money since then.
Cool.
And one of the books you have written is The Acquirer's Multiple that we will discuss today.
Why did you decide to write the book?
Well, I had written quantitative value as sort of a quasi-textbook.
It's, if anybody has read it, it's got some daunting math and algebra in it.
And it's not particularly.
accessible to most investors. It's really for people who are practitioners and who
want that deep dive. And after that, I wrote, there was an unusual phenomenon that we had observed
when we were doing the work, and that was that, and this is common across sort of deep value
where many of the things that you might expect to see in an investment sort of reverses a little
bit when things get very, very undervalued. So, for example, in a net net world, a company
that is an unprofitable net net net tends to outperform a profitable net net.
And similarly, a dividend-paying net net net underperforms a non-dividend paying net net and so on.
So all of these things are very counterintuitive, and there's quite a lot of counterintuitive in
the deepest undervaluation. And partly the reason is that, you know, for the same reason that
you don't want to invest in the very best business. You want to invest in the best
business at the best price. It's sort of more of a handicapping. How much value are you getting
for how much money are you spending? The same idea persists. And so I wrote deep value just to sort of discuss
that idea and the actual mechanics of mean reversion and how participants in the market cause mean reversion
to occur. And I had an opportunity to write a book with some other gentleman called concentrated
investing where we looked at. So stock selection is one part of the problem, but then you
also have a portfolio management issue as well. And you can be a very good stock picker and
not run a very good portfolio because you're overly concentrated in the wrong things or you're not taking
advantage of opportunities when they appear. So concentrated investing, we looked at a lot of the academic
research into portfolio, diversification and concentration. And then we looked at how some
practitioners who had done it, who had been in the markets for a very long period of time,
25 years or more who had succeeded over that period of time running concentrated
books. And what was it that they did that was different from many other investors? And again,
those books were, if you published through this publisher, they're expensive,
all of the books were written to a pretty high reading level. I
subsequently discovered. So I just, after I had written three of these books,
I found that there's a quantitative system for determining the reading level that you need, and it basically equates to what year of schooling you got to. And if you write, and these books were written to sort of second year university level, but if you want to write a book that many people will read, you can't write it above a fifth grade reading level because that cuts out an enormous proportion of the population.
So I wrote, I wanted to write a book that I could give to people who weren't necessarily
familiar with the stock market and I wanted it to be accessible to as many people as possible.
And I also wanted to be able to be read in a very short period of time, like a couple of hours if you sat down and read it in one go.
And so that was the Acquirers Multiple.
It's basically a very brief summary of much of what I had written beforehand in a way that was easy to
read. You didn't need to be a stock market expert. And it sells, I don't know what
the price is now in Amazon. I don't know what it is in Sweden, but it's, you know, the objective,
it was about $10 in the US. So it was supposed to be a pretty cheap book too.
It's very generous of you to share all this knowledge and all the research you have done.
I mean, what was your motivation for sharing that with the public?
Well, I use it, you know, I use it to help market my business and my business is I run two ETFs and estates to exchange-traded funds. One is a mid-cap, large-cap, domestic U.S. Deep Value Fund. The ticker is Zig, ZIG, as in you ZIG when the market's ags. And I run a small and micro-cap version as well, which is called deep, as in deeply undervalued. And both of those funds. And both of those funds,
follow the principles that I have discussed.
They are quantitative, deep value, seeking businesses that are too cheap businesses that are too cheap, might be bought out, and also have, they're at the bottom of their business cycle, rather than the top of their business cycle, because it's one of the traps when you're investing and you look on a multiple or a ratio and you might see that it's cheap relative to its trailing one, three, five years.
but it's because it's a business that's highly cyclical.
And most people in the market realize that it's cyclical.
So lots of, you know, basic materials are extremely cyclical, so iron or even oil or any of those sort of things.
So it's a way of finding things that are cheap, but also cheap on a business that's troughing.
So that's the, and that idea, if you've been investing for a while, I think that idea becomes, you understand that that's what you're attempting to do.
But if you've never invested before, it can be quite daunting to take a look at some of these companies.
And that was one of the things that I found as a money manager that I would show people the portfolio and they'd become very nervous about the portfolio because it looked like it was filled with sort of these very junky companies.
But I would say if you looked at the, they have, they all had very long histories where they had good times and they had bad.
And we were buying them in a bad time.
And so naturally, the.
the history looks bad, or the near history looks bad, but there's always the possibility
that the future could look better. And it doesn't, that doesn't only apply to cyclical businesses.
So, for example, last year, we bought META, which is Facebook. I don't, it's funny how quickly the
attitudes towards businesses change. You don't have to be in the market for very long,
but Facebook was extremely popular at one point. And then it was very
unpopular, not that long ago, a year or two ago. And that was largely because they were spending
spending so much money in the metaverse. But the business remained incredibly robust. It was throwing
off lots of free cash flow that's controlled by one shareholder, essentially Mark Zuckerberg, who
continues to be the primary, the principle of that business. And they were buying back some
stock. And really, that's all that I want, pretty robust business. And of course,
that now it's turned around and it's run back up to close to it. It's all-time highs
and we're out of that position. But that's sort of what we're looking for. We're agnostic to the business.
We'll buy an iron ore miner or a coal mine and we'll equally will buy Facebook. It just depends
a little bit on on where they are in their cycle.
We'll go a bit deeper into your investing style a bit later on in the conversation.
But if we stay on with the book and the acquired
multiple. Maybe you can describe for our listeners the fundamentals of the approach.
The idea is that the acquires multiple itself is, I read this when I was at university, I used to sit in the business
library and read some of the old, this might be even before you guys, but they used to have these
journals and the journals were available on, that they'd come out one after the other in physical
format and they'd put them in these ring binders. And then at some point it
transition to CD-ROM and then it was on the internet. It was on the internet when I got there, but
but none of these old journals had been digitised. They were just sitting in the, in the library and I would
just go through and read them. And one of them had described, it was written during the 1980s,
during the leverage buyout boom in the 1980s, and it described this acquirers multiple,
which was the way that leverage buyout private equity firms thought
about valuing a business.
And the idea was they were looking at, because they can manipulate the capital structure, they can add debt,
or, you know, pay out cash or do lots of other things, they're interested in the operating income
income that's coming into that business.
So operating income, if you think about revenues are, that's the money that comes in from
sales, but then, of course, there's a cost of those sales, the cost of goods sold.
And that leaves you.
with a gross profit, and out of the gross profit comes sale, selling general and administrative
SGNA. And that's the, what it sounds like, selling general and administrative costs of getting
the business to that point. And then from that point on, that money can be directed in various different
ways. And so that's the number that I was interested in. It's the operating income,
which is basically the first point that the company really has any discretion about how
it's going to spend its money. And so it's sometimes called EBIT or EBIT operating
income. They really, they're interchangeable. But I like that construction from the top of the income statement down
because it's harder to manipulate as you get closer and closer to the bottom line. There are many
decisions that management can make, they have a lot of discretion about how they recognize income
and so on. So you can have two companies that are essentially the same that have different
bottom lines, but their operating income is similar. And they should be
compared on a like-for-like basis, but you want to take out all of those decisions that management
have made as you travel down the income statement. And then you have to compare it to something. And so
that's the, that's really what you're getting, that income stream. And what you're giving,
what you're paying is the price of the equity. But anybody who owns a home
knows that the equity that you have in your home is not the entire price of
your home, because when you buy your home, you take out a home loan. And so you might put down 10%.
The mortgage might be 90% of the price that you paid. So that debt needs to be accounted for when
you're thinking about what you're paying. And so we include debt in that calculation. And so this is
the enterprise value of a company is debt plus the equity. And then sometimes you might find a
safe buried inside your house and inside the safe there's some cash. And you get
to keep that cash and you can use that to pay off your business. And so there are these companies out there
that have so much cash on their balance sheet, they have no debt, but they're trading at a discount to cash
naturally because they're losing money. It's never, these aren't great businesses when you find
them like that as you, as it expect. But, you know, that is, that is if you're, if you're,
if you have this private equity or acquirers mindset, you can direct that cash flow
And so you might be able to get control and use that cash.
And so I use enterprise value as the, that's what we're paying.
Operating income is what we're getting.
And the relationship of operating income to enterprise value is known as the acquires multiple.
So that's essentially, and what we found is if you, if you test that idea and you just
buy the cheapest companies on an acquirers multiple basis, they tend to outperform
the next cheapest and so on until you get to the most expensive, which you tend to
underperform everything else over a very long time period, on average, not every year, not every
not every five or 10 years. But that's essentially the big muscle movement that drives the performance
of the portfolio, and that's what the book discusses.
And the book was published in 2017, so your period where you were measuring the performance,
I think it started in 1972 until 2017.
How much was this strategy outperforming the index?
I don't I don't recall exactly what I put in the book or what the test was, but you can see in the book that it had this massive period of outperformance and then a period of underperformance began in 2000, somewhere between 2010 and 2015. There's quite a big drop-off in the chart, which is not uncommon. So I've subsequent to writing the book, I met a gentleman by the name of Michael Samanov, Mikhail Samanov, and he has done this analysis. He calls it two centuries of value.
And so he looked back, I think it was, into the 1800s, in any case, it's a very long period of time.
And he stitched together three data series to create this.
So the one that runs from, there's, there's a data series of a point, the best data that we have is only US base from 1963 until the present day.
And point in time means that they record the financial statements as they issued, not as they are, not for the, so
timing when back testing is always a problem because you you might not know exactly
when a financial statement was issued. And so you might be trading on information that you couldn't have
possibly known at the time. The back test system assumes that you were. So what point in time does is it
makes sure that you're not doing that. And it also retains any companies that go bankrupt in the
database. So you could buy something and it could go bankrupt. So that's the best data
that data actually runs, but before that there's to 1925 is less good data, but still
pretty good data where we've captured balance sheets and so on. From 1925 to 1875 was this thing called
the Cow's Commission where there was a gentleman who was trying to work out whether stock writing newsletters
had any skill. And he used these punch cards and a very ancient
computer to work out whether any of these newsletter writers had any skill.
But that data that came from the Cowes Commission, Benjamin Graham used, in in making his decisions about what went
into security analysis. So that gets us back to 1875. Then from 1875, I think
it's possibly 1825, it might be as early as that. They, somebody has found, somebody has found all of the, all
of the financial statements that they can find, and there aren't a lot around, but they've
been able to find a lot, and they've looked at the dividends that these companies paid because they didn't
have to publish, you know, they weren't, we didn't get cash flow statements, we didn't get income
statements. I think we only got balance sheet, which showed what companies owned, and it wasn't.
There was no obligation to produce this stuff. But you could see dividend payments
they were known and they were real. And that's also a way of assessing value if something's
got a high dividend yield that's cheap relative to its dividend payments. And so they use that data.
So I just, I go into that detail to see the old data is obviously, it's not as good as the current data,
but you can still see these, it's, it still behaves exactly the way you'd expect in relation to
value. The cheapest stuff tends to outperform the more expensive stuff. But there
are some very interesting things that become observable in this data, and that is there are all of these
recessions and depressions and technology booms that occurred hundreds of years ago that we've largely forgotten
about. And one example is there was a thing known as the Great Depression before the 1929 Great Depression.
When the 1929 Great Depression was called the Great Depression, they had to change the name
of the old Great Depression, and so it's now known as the Long Depression.
But there are quite a few.
It's not, it's not, and they all have these, there must have been, you know, famous kind of depressions, the way that we think about the 1929 Great Depression.
But it's interesting to watch, you can see these little technology bubbles and these technology booms along the way.
And the first technology boom is the steam engine.
And so the steam engine is about 1825, and that's Commodore Vanderbilt has these steam boats.
And so there's a fad for steam and those steam engines become very popular.
And then in 1844, there is a technology boom, which is the, which is the telegraph that laid a cable from, I think, from New York to London, a subsidy cable.
And before then, information travel, as fast as the wind did across that.
So there were genuine arbitrages.
You could be a gold arbitrage.
And there was such a big difference in the price between London, New York.
you could make money doing that. Whereas when the, when the cable came in, it became much more difficult
because the price is sort of largely normalized. What that long history shows is that there are these very long
periods of underperformance of value. And they're typically associated with these technology booms or these
manias in the stock market. And there have been many. But there are six very long periods
of value underperformance going back to about 1825. And one of them happens to be
be from about 2010 until about 2020, midway through 2020. So the book was written in

much better. But the book, I'll have to write an update to the book where I show the eventual
turn around. But I find it, I find it fascinating because it feels like an extremely long period of time
to underperform from 2010 to 2020. But in the very long history, it's, it's not that long
at all. I mean, it's quite tough. I mean, that figure in terms of active managers, I mean, that figure in terms of active
managers, I mean, in 10 years, you would be gone. Right. You wouldn't have a job.
And that's true. There've been many, many value managers who've shut down and
have disappeared. And if you think about the value managers who are well known
And today, most of them tend to be people who established their reputation before 2010.
There are many from the early 2000s and there are many from before then, but there really aren't very many
since 2010. It would be very hard to name any value managers who've done well.
So David Ironhorn, of course, was pre-2010. Dan Loeb is pre-2010.
Bill Ackman is pre-2010. Monish-Prii pre-2010.
Guy Speart, pre-2010. Since 2010, they
there's nobody, really.
In the second episode of Investing By the Books, we spoke to your good friend, Jake Taylor, about his book,
The Rebel Allocator, and that Charlie Munger had asked him to make a movie out of it.
And then we asked him, like, is this on the table now? And he said, well, we need to find some money
and maybe the value community can support it, what's left of us.
And it wasn't much. At the time, it felt like there was no, not many
value investors left, but now it's, the wind is changing. So, so this quantitative approach
that you're mentioning, I mean, many of our listeners are familiar with Joel Greenblatt's work and,
and the magic formula, and you also compare it to, to that work in your book. So maybe you can talk a bit

the little book that beat the market. I bought that when it first came out in about
2005 and read it and loved it because I, you know, you can read Buffett's letters
letters and get an idea of his approach, but to my knowledge, nobody had quantitatively tested what he

And Greenblatt did that. He looked at two metrics, so Buffett is well known for saying
that he likes a wonderful company at a fair price.
a fair price. He uses what he calls the earnings yield, which is the inverse of
the acquires multiple. It's EBIT on enterprise value. It really makes no difference whether you take
which way around that ratio goes just so long as you remember that you're taking the high ratio in one way.
You preferring a high number in one and a low number in the other. And then he compared
compared it to the wonderful company metric is the, again, the EBIT or the operating

bit. So the reasons why you might still persist with the magic formula over just a pure
value approach is exactly what we've then subsequently gone through, which is that in a very bullish, bubbly market,
these companies that have the very high returns on invested capital tend to outperform.
And there's a research report called the little note that beats the market.
And I'm just blanking on the name of the author, but I hope that will come back to me

might be so long that it's impossible for an investor to sort of sustain
to stay in this strategy or for a manager to retain their job.
